title: ANCHOR in New Jersey: what seniors get and how to file
dek: ANCHOR pays New Jersey homeowners up to $1,500 and senior renters $700. If you are 65 or older and own your home, you have to file the PAS-1 yourself by November 2, 2026.
keyFacts: 2025 benefit: $1,500 for homeowners with income up to $150,000
$1,000 for homeowners with income from $150,001 to $250,000
Renters: $700 at 65 or older, $450 if younger (income up to $150,000)
Seniors who own must file the PAS-1 by November 2, 2026
body:
ANCHOR is New Jersey's biggest property tax relief program. The name stands for Affordable New Jersey Communities for Homeowners and Renters. It sends a yearly payment to people who own or rent their main home in the state. You do not need to have a low income. Homeowners can earn up to $250,000 and still qualify.

For older adults, the most important thing to know is simple. If you are 65 or older and own your home, the state did not file for you. You have to file the combined Application for Property Tax Relief, called the PAS-1. The deadline for 2025 benefits is November 2, 2026.

How much does ANCHOR pay?

The amount depends on whether you own or rent, your income and, for renters, your age. Income here means New Jersey gross income, the figure on line 29 of your NJ-1040 state tax return.

Who you are2025 income2025 ANCHOR benefit
Homeowner, any age$150,000 or less$1,500
Homeowner, any age$150,001 to $250,000$1,000
Renter, 65 or older by December 31, 2025$150,000 or less$700
Renter, 64 or younger$150,000 or less$450

Senior renters get an extra $250, which is how they reach $700. Homeowners get the same amount at any age. One small bonus: if you were 65 or older and did not claim the $50 Property Tax Credit on a state tax return, the state adds that credit to your ANCHOR payment.

If you are 65 or older and own your home, nobody filed for you. You have to file.

Who qualifies?

Homeowners

Your home must be your main residence in New Jersey, and your 2025 New Jersey gross income must be $250,000 or less. Condo owners who pay property taxes on their unit count as homeowners. So do resident shareholders in a co-op, and residents of continuing care communities whose contracts make them pay their share of the unit's property taxes.

Some homes do not count. Vacation homes, second homes and property you rent out to others are excluded. If your home is fully exempt from property taxes, you cannot get the homeowner benefit.

Renters

The rental must have been your main home on October 1, 2025, and your income must be $150,000 or less. Renting a condo, a co-op unit or a mobile home in a mobile home park all qualify. Units in tax-exempt housing owned by a government agency, or homes owned by religious, charitable or nonprofit groups, generally do not.

Do I have to file, or will the state do it?

It depends on your age and whether you own. The state filed automatically for most eligible homeowners under 65 and for most eligible renters of all ages, and mailed them a letter. If you rent and got that letter, you are likely set. If you rent and did not get one, you can file yourself.

Homeowners 65 and older, and people collecting Social Security or Railroad Retirement disability benefits, were not filed automatically. The state says plainly that it will not file for you. You must use the PAS-1, even if you only qualify for ANCHOR.

One form, three programs

The PAS-1 also covers Senior Freeze and Stay NJ. Filing once checks you for all three. Read our Senior Freeze guide and Stay NJ guide, or the complete property tax relief guide for how they stack.

How do I file the PAS-1?

You can file online at propertytaxreliefapp.nj.gov or on a paper form. The online application asks you to verify your identity, so have a photo ID ready.

  1. Find your property tax bills. You may need details from both your 2024 and 2025 bills, such as your block and lot.
  2. Pull your income records. Your 2024 and 2025 NJ-1040 returns if you filed, and proof of Social Security. The state suggests a my Social Security account as the fastest way to get your benefit statement.
  3. Check the income rules. The PAS-1 instructions explain which disability payments count as income.
  4. Choose how to be paid. Online filers can pick direct deposit or a paper check. Paper filers get a check.
  5. Submit and keep a copy. Save your confirmation number or a photocopy of the paper form.

Need a hand? Call the Property Tax Relief line at 1-888-238-1233. It runs around the clock, with live agents from 8:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. You can also call 609-826-4282 during those hours, book a telephone appointment, or visit a Division of Taxation Regional Information Center. The Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 can point you to a free filing event near you.

When will the money arrive?

ANCHOR payments for 2025 began on a rolling basis on September 15, 2026. Most people are paid within 90 days of filing, unless the state needs more information. If a letter arrives asking for something, answer it fast. A pending question holds up your payment.

Your total property tax relief from all programs can never be more than the property taxes you paid on your home for the year. If you receive a check you know you should not have, mail it to the New Jersey Division of Taxation, PO Box 266, Trenton, NJ 08695-0266.

Example: a renter in Hackensack

Say you are 78, rent an apartment and have income of $38,000 in 2025. You qualify for $700. If you did not file a state tax return, the state may add the $50 Property Tax Credit. Senior Freeze and Stay NJ are for homeowners, so ANCHOR is your benefit here.

What mistakes should I avoid?

  • Assuming you were filed automatically. Senior homeowners were not. Check your mail and your status online.
  • Waiting for the last day. Identity checks and busy phone lines take time.
  • Answering texts or emails about rebates. Go straight to nj.gov. Our guide to scams in New Jersey explains the warning signs.
  • Forgetting next year. You file a new PAS-1 every year.

If money is tight in other areas too, see our guides to prescription and bill help and food and utility help.

faq.q: What is the ANCHOR deadline for 2025 benefits?
faq.a: The deadline to file the PAS-1 for 2025 benefits is November 2, 2026. Seniors who own their homes must file it themselves.

faq.q: How much is ANCHOR for seniors in 2026?
faq.a: For 2025 benefits paid in 2026, homeowners get $1,500 with income up to $150,000 or $1,000 from $150,001 to $250,000. Renters 65 or older get $700 with income up to $150,000.

faq.q: Do senior homeowners get extra ANCHOR money?
faq.a: No. Homeowners get the same amount at any age. Renters who were 65 or older by December 31, 2025, get an extra $250, for a total of $700.

faq.q: I rent and I am over 65. Do I need to file?
faq.a: The state filed automatically for most eligible renters and mailed them a letter. If you did not get a letter, file the application yourself by November 2, 2026.

faq.q: When are ANCHOR payments sent?
faq.a: Payments began on a rolling basis on September 15, 2026. Most people are paid within 90 days of filing unless the state needs more information.

faq.q: Who can help me file?
faq.a: Call the Property Tax Relief line at 1-888-238-1233 or 609-826-4282. You can also book a telephone appointment or visit a Division of Taxation Regional Information Center.

title: Senior Freeze in NJ: how the property tax reimbursement works
dek: Senior Freeze pays you back when your property taxes rise above your base year. Here are the 2025 rules, the income limits and how to keep your base year safe.
keyFacts: Age 65 or older by December 31, 2025, or on Social Security disability
Owned and lived in your home since December 31, 2022
Income limits: $168,268 for 2024 and $172,475 for 2025
File the PAS-1 by November 2, 2026
Senior Freeze line: 1-800-882-6597
body:
Senior Freeze is the common name for New Jersey's Property Tax Reimbursement program. It does not literally freeze your tax bill. You still pay your taxes in full. Then the state pays you back the amount your taxes went up since your base year.

If your taxes have climbed for years, the check can add up. If your taxes have not gone up, you get nothing from this program, though you may still get ANCHOR and Stay NJ on the same form.

Who qualifies for 2025?

  • Age or disability. You or your spouse or civil union partner must have been 65 or older by December 31, 2025, or you must have received federal Social Security or Railroad Retirement disability benefits for yourself on or before that date.
  • Ownership. You must have owned and lived in your New Jersey home since December 31, 2022, and still owned and lived there on December 31, 2025.
  • Income. Your total income must be $168,268 or less for 2024 and $172,475 or less for 2025. Couples living together combine their income.
  • Every year counts. You must meet the rules for each year from your base year through the application year.

Mobile home owners can qualify too. You must have leased a site in a mobile home park for a home you have owned since December 31, 2022, and be subject to site fees. The reimbursement then covers increases in your site fees.

What counts as income?

Senior Freeze counts more than your state tax return does. That surprises people. Federal Social Security counts. So do tax-exempt interest, distributions from or rollovers to a Roth IRA, and some retirement income that is not taxed, such as a disability pension. Traditional IRA rollovers that are not taxable in New Jersey are left out.

So check the numbers even if you easily passed the ANCHOR income test. The PAS-1 instructions include worksheets to help you add it up.

How is the reimbursement figured?

The math is one line. Take the property taxes billed for the application year and subtract the taxes billed for your base year. The difference is your reimbursement. If you co-own the home with someone other than your spouse, the benefit is based on your share of ownership.

Example: a homeowner in Toms River

Say your base year tax bill was $6,900 and your 2025 bill was $7,600. Your Senior Freeze reimbursement would be $700. Your total relief from all three programs can never be more than the property taxes you paid that year.

What if I co-own the home or live in a two-family?

Ownership shares matter. If you own the home with someone other than your spouse or civil union partner, such as a sibling or an adult child, your reimbursement is based on your percentage of ownership. Enter that share carefully on the PAS-1.

If you own a multiunit property and live in one unit, the benefit is based on the share of property taxes for the part you live in. Condos, co-ops and continuing care retirement communities do not count as multiunit properties for this rule.

Why does the base year matter so much?

Your base year is the year your taxes were frozen for this program. Every later year is compared to it. The lower your base year bill, the bigger your reimbursement as taxes rise.

The state says continuity matters. If your eligibility is interrupted, you must set a new base year, usually at a higher tax level. If your income goes over the limit after you have received a freeze, you are not reimbursed that year. As a one-time exception, you can keep your base year for the next application if you meet every other rule. If it happens again, you start over with a new base year.

File every year. A missed year can cost you your base year.

How do I apply?

Senior Freeze is part of the combined Application for Property Tax Relief, the PAS-1. The same form covers ANCHOR and Stay NJ. The deadline for 2025 benefits is November 2, 2026. The state does not file it for you.

  1. Gather both tax bills. Senior Freeze needs your 2024 and 2025 property tax information.
  2. Collect income records for both years. NJ-1040 returns if you filed, your SSA-1099 forms and any Roth or pension statements.
  3. File online or on paper. Online filing is at propertytaxreliefapp.nj.gov and asks you to verify your identity.
  4. Check your status. Use the state's online status tool, and answer any letter quickly.

You do not have to do this alone. The Division of Taxation holds PAS-1 filing events around the state where staff help you fill out the application. You can also visit a Regional Information Center or book a telephone appointment. Many county offices on aging host help sessions too.

For help, call the Senior Freeze information line at 1-800-882-6597 or the Property Tax Relief line at 1-888-238-1233.

When are Senior Freeze checks mailed?

Checks for 2025 benefits are paid by check on a schedule based on when you filed. The state mailed its first round on July 15, 2026, to more than 188,000 seniors.

Application filedChecks begin
Before May 1, 2026July 15, 2026
May 1 to June 1, 2026September 1, 2026
June 2 to September 1, 2026November 2, 2026
September 2 to October 31, 2026December 1, 2026

The schedule does not list a date for applications filed in the final days before the deadline, so check your status online after you file. If the state overpays you, you must repay the extra.

What mistakes cost people money?

  • Skipping a year and losing the base year.
  • Leaving out Social Security on the income lines.
  • Entering only one year of tax figures.
  • Thinking Senior Freeze is automatic. It never is.

For how Senior Freeze fits with the other two programs, read our complete property tax relief guide, plus our pages on ANCHOR and Stay NJ.

faq.q: What is the Senior Freeze income limit for 2025 benefits?
faq.a: Your income must be $168,268 or less for 2024 and $172,475 or less for 2025. Married couples and civil union partners living together combine their income.

faq.q: Does Senior Freeze count Social Security?
faq.a: Yes. Federal Social Security counts as income for Senior Freeze, along with some other items the state income tax ignores, such as tax-exempt interest and Roth IRA distributions.

faq.q: How long do I need to own my home?
faq.a: For 2025 benefits, you must have owned and lived in your New Jersey home since December 31, 2022, and still owned and lived there on December 31, 2025.

faq.q: What happens if I miss a year?
faq.a: You must meet the rules every year from your base year onward. If eligibility is interrupted, you generally have to set a new base year, which can lower future reimbursements.

faq.q: When is the Senior Freeze deadline?
faq.a: File the PAS-1 by November 2, 2026, for 2025 benefits. It also covers ANCHOR and Stay NJ.

faq.q: What is the Senior Freeze phone number?
faq.a: The Senior Freeze information line is 1-800-882-6597. The Property Tax Relief line is 1-888-238-1233.

title: Stay NJ: how the senior property tax benefit works
dek: Stay NJ aims to cover half of a senior homeowner's property taxes, up to $6,500. Here is who qualifies for 2025, how the math works and when payments arrive.
keyFacts: For homeowners 65 or older in 2025 with income up to $200,000
Brings total relief up to 50% of your property taxes
Maximums: $6,500, $5,000 or $4,000 depending on income
2025 benefit paid in February and May 2027
File the PAS-1 by November 2, 2026
body:
Stay NJ is New Jersey's newest property tax program for older homeowners. Its goal is in the name. The state wants to make it easier for seniors to stay in the homes they own. It does that by bringing your total property tax relief up to half of your tax bill, within a cap set by your income.

You apply for it on the same form as ANCHOR and Senior Freeze, the PAS-1. The deadline for 2025 benefits is November 2, 2026.

Who qualifies for 2025?

  • Age. You must have been 65 or older during 2025. For a married couple, one spouse meeting the age rule is enough.
  • Ownership. You must have owned and lived in your home for the full 12 months of 2025.
  • Property taxes. The home must be subject to property taxes or to payments in lieu of taxes (P.I.L.O.T.).
  • Income. Your total 2025 income must be $200,000 or less. Income is figured the same way as for Senior Freeze, so it includes Social Security. Couples living together combine their income.

Renters and mobile home owners are not eligible for Stay NJ. Senior renters can still get ANCHOR.

How much could I get?

Your maximum depends on your income. The state lists these annual maximums for the 2025 benefit, paid in 2027:

2025 incomeMaximum Stay NJ benefit
$100,000 or less$6,500
$100,000.01 to $150,000$5,000
$150,000.01 to $200,000$4,000
Over $200,000Not eligible

The state notes that these maximums are shown on an annual basis and assume no changes to Stay NJ in the Fiscal Year 2028 state budget.

How does Stay NJ work with ANCHOR and Senior Freeze?

The state figures the three programs in order. ANCHOR comes first. Senior Freeze comes second. Stay NJ is last. It fills the gap between what the first two pay and half of your property taxes, up to your cap.

  • If ANCHOR and Senior Freeze together pay less than half your taxes, Stay NJ makes up the difference, within your maximum.
  • If ANCHOR and Senior Freeze already pay half or more, you get nothing from Stay NJ.

That means you cannot add the three maximums together. Your total relief also can never be more than the taxes you paid.

Example 1: a couple in Wayne

Say you are 70 and 72 with 2025 income of $90,000, and your property taxes were $11,000. You have owned the home for 20 years. Half your taxes is $5,500, which is under your $6,500 cap. ANCHOR pays $1,500 and Senior Freeze pays $800. Together that is $2,300. Stay NJ adds $3,200, for total relief of $5,500.

Example 2: a widow in Princeton

Say you are 75, your 2025 income was $160,000 and your taxes were $16,000. Half your taxes would be $8,000, but your income puts your cap at $4,000. If ANCHOR pays $1,000 and you get no Senior Freeze, Stay NJ adds $3,000 to reach $4,000.

Example 3: a longtime owner in Ocean City

Say you are 81, your income was $45,000 and your taxes were $4,000. Half your taxes is $2,000. ANCHOR pays $1,500 and Senior Freeze pays $700, a total of $2,200. That is already more than half your taxes, so Stay NJ adds nothing. You still come out ahead from the first two programs.

These are hypothetical round numbers. Your benefit statement from the state will show your real figures for each program.

When will I be paid?

Stay NJ is paid by check in quarterly installments. The state says the 2025 benefit will be paid in February and May of 2027. The Fiscal Year 2027 budget, signed on June 30, 2026, funds Stay NJ for applicants with incomes of $200,000 or less.

You may still be receiving 2024 benefits. The state split the third quarter 2024 payment into two halves, paid in August and November 2026. That change means recipients get a lower overall benefit for calendar year 2026. Your status page at propertytaxreliefstatus.nj.gov shows what you are owed.

Stay NJ depends on the state budget each year. File anyway, and file every year.

How do I apply?

File the PAS-1 online at propertytaxreliefapp.nj.gov or on paper. The state will not file for you if you are 65 or older.

  1. Get your 2025 property tax bill and your 2024 bill too, since the same form handles Senior Freeze.
  2. Add up your 2025 income, including Social Security. Use your SSA-1099 or a my Social Security account.
  3. Answer the ownership questions carefully, including your share if you co-own the home.
  4. Submit by November 2, 2026, and keep your confirmation.

For help, call the Property Tax Relief line at 1-888-238-1233 (live agents 8:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.) or 609-826-4282. The Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 can point you to free filing help nearby.

How do I check my benefit?

Every applicant receives a benefit statement that lists the Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ amounts separately. You can also look up your 2025 benefit details on the state's online status system. Keep the statement with your tax papers. If the numbers look wrong, call the Property Tax Relief line and have your statement in front of you.

Because Stay NJ is figured last, a change in one program changes it too. For example, if your Senior Freeze amount is adjusted after review, your Stay NJ amount may move in the other direction.

What should I watch out for?

  • Buying or moving during 2025. You must have owned and lived in the home for all 12 months.
  • Undercounting income. Stay NJ uses the broader Senior Freeze income definition.
  • Fake rebate messages. The state does not text you for your bank details. See our scams guide.

For the full picture, read our complete property tax relief guide and our page on Senior Freeze. If you are weighing whether to stay put long term, see aging in place in New Jersey.

faq.q: Who is eligible for Stay NJ?
faq.a: Homeowners who were 65 or older during 2025, owned and lived in the home all 12 months of 2025, and had total income of $200,000 or less. Renters and mobile home owners are not eligible.

faq.q: How much is the Stay NJ benefit?
faq.a: It brings your total property tax relief up to half of your taxes, with a maximum of $6,500 for income up to $100,000, $5,000 up to $150,000 and $4,000 up to $200,000.

faq.q: When will Stay NJ payments arrive for 2025?
faq.a: The state says the 2025 benefit will be paid in quarterly installments in February and May of 2027.

faq.q: Do I need a separate application for Stay NJ?
faq.a: No. Stay NJ is part of the PAS-1, which also covers ANCHOR and Senior Freeze. File it by November 2, 2026.

faq.q: Does Stay NJ count Social Security as income?
faq.a: Yes. Stay NJ uses the same income rules as Senior Freeze, which include federal Social Security.

title: PAAD in New Jersey: $5 and $7 prescriptions for seniors
dek: PAAD cuts prescription copays to $5 for generics and $7 for brand names. Here is who qualifies in 2026, how it works with Medicare Part D and how to apply.
keyFacts: 2026 income: under $54,943 single, under $62,390 married
Copays: $5 generic, $7 brand name
Age 65 or older, or 18 to 64 on Social Security disability
Pays some Part D premiums at or below the regional benchmark
body:
Pharmaceutical Assistance to the Aged and Disabled, known as PAAD, is one of New Jersey's best deals for older adults. If you qualify, you pay $5 for a covered generic prescription and $7 for a covered brand name drug. For someone on several medicines, that can save thousands of dollars a year.

The income limit is higher than many people expect. Plenty of retirees with a pension and Social Security still qualify.

Who qualifies for PAAD in 2026?

  • Residence. You must live in New Jersey.
  • Age or disability. You must be 65 or older, or 18 to 64 and receiving Social Security Title II disability benefits.
  • Income. Your 2026 income must be less than $54,943 if you are single, or less than $62,390 if you are married.

You cannot get PAAD if you receive Medicaid. You also cannot get it if you have health insurance or retiree benefits with prescription coverage that is as good as or better than PAAD. Limited or partial drug coverage does not rule you out.

Under $54,943 single or $62,390 married? Check PAAD before you assume you earn too much.

How does PAAD work with Medicare Part D?

If you have Medicare, you must be enrolled in a Part D drug plan. PAAD works on top of it.

  • Premiums. PAAD pays the monthly premium for certain standard basic Part D plans priced at or below the regional benchmark. If you pick an enhanced plan at or below the benchmark, PAAD pays the premium as long as the plan follows the billing rules.
  • Medicare Advantage. If you are in a Medicare Advantage plan, it must include drug coverage. PAAD contributes up to the regional benchmark toward the drug part of your premium.
  • Copays. You pay $5 or $7. If your Part D plan charges less than $5 for a generic, you pay the lower amount.
  • Formulary. If a drug is not on your plan's list, switch to one that is, or ask your doctor to request a medical necessity exception from the plan.
Shopping for a Part D plan?

Medicare open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7. If you choose a plan priced above the benchmark, you may owe part of the premium. Free counselors at the State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) can compare plans with you at 1-800-792-8820. They do not sell insurance.

What does PAAD cover, and what does it not?

PAAD covers prescription drugs, insulin and insulin supplies, and needles and syringes for injectable multiple sclerosis medicines.

It does not cover:

  • Diabetic testing supplies such as strips and lancets. If you have Medicare Part B, the pharmacy bills Part B for those.
  • Drugs bought outside New Jersey.
  • Drugs not approved by the FDA.
  • Products whose makers have not agreed to give New Jersey rebates.

A few pharmacy rules to know

  • Generics first. When an approved generic exists, the pharmacy must use it. To get the brand name, your prescriber must request prior authorization.
  • Supply limits. A first prescription is limited to a 34-day supply. Refills can be up to a 34-day supply or 100 unit doses, whichever is greater.
  • Safety checks. A drug review looks for harmful interactions, dosing problems and duplicate prescriptions.

How do I apply?

Apply through NJSave, the state's single application for older adults and people with disabilities. One form screens you for PAAD, Senior Gold, Lifeline utility help, the Medicare Savings Programs, Extra Help and hearing aid help. It also checks you for heating aid, the Universal Service Fund and SNAP food benefits.

Apply online at the NJSave application. A paper version is available too. For help, call 1-800-792-9745, your county office on aging, or SHIP.

  1. Gather proof of income for you and your spouse: Social Security statements, pensions and interest.
  2. Have your Medicare card and Part D plan name handy.
  3. Answer every question, including the Lifeline questions. They add $225 a year toward utilities.
  4. Watch your mail for your ID card or a request for documents.
Example: a widower in Cherry Hill

Say you are 74, single, with $31,000 from Social Security and $14,000 from a pension. At $45,000, you are under the $54,943 limit. If you take four brand name drugs a month, you would pay $28 a month in copays, and PAAD could pay your premium for a basic Part D plan at or below the benchmark.

What else comes with PAAD?

  • Lifeline. $225 a year toward electric and gas bills, with the same age and income rules. Do not apply if you receive SSI, since your check already includes a utility supplement.
  • Other perks. The state says people who qualify for PAAD and Lifeline may also be eligible for reduced motor vehicle fees and low-cost spaying and neutering for pets.
  • Winter shutoff protection. PAAD members qualify for the state's Winter Termination Program. See our LIHEAP guide.

How do I keep my PAAD?

Most members renew every two years, and some every year. A renewal form arrives about four months before your card expires. Fill it out and mail it back. If it has not come at least two months before your card expires, call 1-800-792-9745.

What mistakes should I avoid?

  • Assuming you earn too much. The limit is close to $55,000 for one person. Check before you skip it.
  • Filling prescriptions out of state. PAAD does not cover drugs bought outside New Jersey. Plan ahead before a long trip.
  • Ignoring the formulary. If your Part D plan drops a drug, PAAD will not fill the gap until you switch or get an exception.
  • Missing the renewal form. Mark your card's expiration date on the calendar.

If your income is a little over the PAAD limit, look at Senior Gold. For the Medicare Savings Programs and Extra Help, read our guide to prescription and bill help.

faq.q: What is the PAAD income limit for 2026?
faq.a: Your income must be less than $54,943 if single or less than $62,390 if married. You must be 65 or older, or 18 to 64 and receiving Social Security disability.

faq.q: What are PAAD copays?
faq.a: You pay $5 for each covered generic prescription and $7 for each covered brand name drug. If your Part D plan charges less than $5 for a generic, you pay the lower amount.

faq.q: Do I need Medicare Part D to get PAAD?
faq.a: Yes, if you have Medicare. PAAD pays the premium for certain basic Part D plans at or below the regional benchmark and covers your costs beyond the copay.

faq.q: Can I have PAAD and Medicaid?
faq.a: No. People who receive Medicaid are not eligible for PAAD.

faq.q: Does PAAD cover diabetic test strips?
faq.a: No. PAAD covers insulin and insulin supplies, but test strips and lancets go through Medicare Part B or other coverage.

faq.q: How do I apply for PAAD?
faq.a: Apply through NJSave online or on paper. Call 1-800-792-9745 for help or to ask for a paper application.

title: Senior Gold in NJ: prescription help above the PAAD limit
dek: Earn a little too much for PAAD? Senior Gold cuts what you pay for each prescription and caps your yearly costs. Here are the 2026 income ranges and how it works.
keyFacts: 2026 income: $54,943 to $64,943 single, $62,390 to $72,390 married
You pay $15 plus 50% of the remaining cost
After $2,000 out of pocket ($3,000 married), a flat $15
You keep paying your own Part D premium
body:
Senior Gold is New Jersey's prescription discount program for people who earn just over the PAAD limit. It is less generous than PAAD, but it still cuts drug costs, and it puts a ceiling on what you pay in a year. If you missed PAAD by a few thousand dollars, Senior Gold is the next place to look.

Who qualifies in 2026?

  • Residence. You must live in New Jersey.
  • Age or disability. You must be 65 or older, or at least 18 and receiving Social Security disability benefits.
  • Income. Your 2026 annual income must be between $54,943 and $64,943 if you are single, or between $62,390 and $72,390 if you are married.
ProgramSingleMarried
PAADUnder $54,943Under $62,390
Senior Gold$54,943 to $64,943$62,390 to $72,390

If your income is below the Senior Gold range, read our PAAD guide instead. PAAD costs you less.

What will I pay at the pharmacy?

For each covered prescription, you pay $15 plus 50% of the remaining cost. Once your out-of-pocket costs pass $2,000 in your eligibility period, or $3,000 for a married couple, you pay a flat $15 for each prescription for the rest of that period.

How the copay math works

Say a covered prescription costs $115. You pay the first $15. The remaining cost is $100, and you pay half of it, $50. Your total is $65. After you pass the $2,000 threshold (single), that same prescription would cost you $15.

Senior Gold puts a ceiling on a bad year. After the threshold, every covered prescription is $15.

How is Senior Gold different from PAAD?

PAADSenior Gold
Copay$5 generic, $7 brand$15 plus 50% of the remaining cost
Yearly ceilingCopays stay at $5 and $7Flat $15 after $2,000 out of pocket ($3,000 married)
Part D premiumPaid for certain plans at or below the benchmarkYou pay it
RenewalMost every two yearsEvery year

Both programs use the same application, the same hotline and the same age and disability rules. The difference is income, and how much of the cost you carry.

How does Senior Gold work with Medicare?

If you are eligible for Medicare, you must be in a Part D drug plan. Senior Gold works alongside it. Two important differences from PAAD:

  • You pay your own premium. Senior Gold members pay the monthly Part D premium directly to their plan. PAAD pays some premiums, Senior Gold does not.
  • Late penalties are yours. If you owe a Medicare late enrollment penalty for months you could have joined Part D and did not, you pay it.

Because you pay the premium, plan choice matters more. During Medicare open enrollment, October 15 to December 7, compare plans that cover your drugs. The State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) offers free, unbiased help at 1-800-792-8820.

Example: a couple in Freehold

Say you are both retired, with combined income of $68,000 from Social Security and a pension. That is over the $62,390 PAAD limit for couples but inside the Senior Gold range. You keep your own Part D plan and premium, pay $15 plus half the remaining cost per prescription, and drop to $15 each once your out-of-pocket costs pass $3,000.

Example: a retired teacher in Toms River

Say you are 70, single, with income of $60,000, and you take an expensive brand name drug every month. Early in your eligibility period you pay $15 plus half the remaining cost for each fill. Once your out-of-pocket total passes $2,000, each fill drops to $15 for the rest of the period. For people with costly medicines, that ceiling is the main benefit.

How do I apply?

Use NJSave, the same application used for PAAD. One form screens you for Senior Gold, PAAD, Lifeline, the Medicare Savings Programs, Extra Help and hearing aid help. It also checks you for heating aid, the Universal Service Fund and SNAP.

Apply online at the NJSave application, or print the paper application. For help, call 1-800-792-9745 or your county office on aging.

  1. Add up household income from Social Security, pensions, interest and any work.
  2. Have your Medicare card and Part D plan details ready.
  3. Complete NJSave and answer every section, even if you think a program does not fit.
  4. Look for your card. If approved, your ID card should arrive within 30 days.

What if my income is right at the line?

Apply anyway. NJSave enrolls eligible applicants into whichever program fits. If your income is under the PAAD limit, you will be placed in PAAD, which costs you less. If it is above the Senior Gold range, the same application can still screen you for other help, such as the Medicare Savings Programs or Extra Help, which use different rules.

Questions to ask when you call

  • Which income counts for my household, and for which year?
  • When does my eligibility period start and end?
  • How do I track my out-of-pocket total toward the threshold?
  • Can you mail me a paper application?

How do I stay enrolled?

Senior Gold members must reapply every year. The renewal form arrives about four months before your card expires. Mail it back promptly. If it has not arrived at least two months before your card expires, call 1-800-792-9745.

What mistakes should I avoid?

  • Skipping the renewal. Senior Gold is yearly, unlike most PAAD memberships.
  • Picking a plan on premium alone. Check that your drugs are on the plan's list.
  • Not reapplying when income drops. If your income falls under the PAAD limit, you could move to the cheaper program.
  • Ignoring other help. Read our guide to prescription and bill help for Extra Help and the Medicare Savings Programs, which have their own rules.

faq.a: Income must be between $54,943 and $64,943 if single, or between $62,390 and $72,390 if married.

faq.q: How much do Senior Gold members pay for prescriptions?
faq.a: You pay $15 plus 50% of the remaining cost of each covered drug. After $2,000 in out-of-pocket costs ($3,000 for couples), you pay a flat $15 per prescription.

faq.q: Does Senior Gold pay my Part D premium?
faq.a: No. Senior Gold members pay their Part D premium directly to their plan. PAAD, which has lower income limits, pays some premiums.

faq.q: How often do I renew Senior Gold?
faq.a: Every year. A renewal form arrives about four months before your card expires. Call 1-800-792-9745 if it has not come two months before.

faq.q: How long does Senior Gold approval take?
faq.a: If you are approved, the state says your ID card should arrive within 30 days.

title: LIHEAP in New Jersey: help with heating and cooling bills
dek: One application covers heating aid, monthly bill credits and medically necessary cooling. Here are the 2026 to 2027 income limits and how older adults can apply by mail.
keyFacts: Apply October 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027, first come, first served
Income limit: $51,273 for one person, $67,049 for two
Medically necessary cooling: $300
USF credits up to $200 a month
body:
The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP, helps New Jersey households pay to heat and cool their homes. The same application also covers the Universal Service Fund (USF), which lowers monthly gas and electric bills. If your heating bill keeps you up at night, this is the first call to make.

For the 2027 federal fiscal year, applications are open from October 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027. Help is first come, first served, so applying early matters.

Who qualifies?

Your household must be responsible for heating or cooling costs, either directly or through your rent. Your gross income must be at or below 60% of the state median income. There is no age requirement, but many applicants are older adults on fixed incomes.

Household sizeMonthly income limitAnnual income limit
1$4,273$51,273
2$5,587$67,049
3$6,902$82,825
4$8,217$98,602

Larger households have higher limits. The state's fact sheet lists limits for larger households. To get USF, you also need a residential electric or gas bill in the name of someone in the household.

A single person can earn up to $51,273 and still qualify. Many retirees do.

What help can I get?

Heating assistance

The amount depends on your income, household size, fuel type and region of the state. How it is paid depends on how you heat:

  • Gas or electric heat. The benefit may go straight to your utility.
  • Oil, propane or another delivered fuel. You generally get a check made out to you and your fuel supplier.
  • Heat included in rent. You get a check made out to you.

If you live in public housing or get rental assistance, you are not eligible for heating help unless you pay a fuel supplier directly.

Medically necessary cooling

If someone in the home needs air conditioning for health reasons, the program pays a fixed $300. It is usually a credit on an active electric account, or a check if that is not possible.

Universal Service Fund

USF helps pay gas and electric costs above a set share of your income, based on how you heat. Credits can reach up to $200 a month. The LIHEAP application doubles as a USF application, so you can get both at once.

Emergency help

The Department of Community Affairs also lists emergency heating system services and emergency fuel assistance as part of the program. If your heat is out or your tank is empty, call 1-800-510-3102 right away and say so.

How do I apply?

You can apply online at energyassistance.nj.gov, or through a local application agency in your county. Call 1-800-510-3102 to find yours.

Applying at 60 or older

If you are 60 or older, or have a disability, you can get and return the application by mail. You can also ask the agency in your county for a home visit if you need one.

  1. Gather income proof for everyone in the household: Social Security award letters, pension statements and pay stubs.
  2. Find your bills. A recent gas or electric bill, plus oil or propane delivery receipts if you have them.
  3. Show your housing costs with a lease or property tax bill.
  4. Apply once online, by mail or in person. Ask about weatherization while you are at it.
  5. Respond fast to any request for missing papers.
Example: a widow in Vineland

Say you are 76, live alone and get $2,000 a month from Social Security. You heat with oil. At $24,000 a year, you are well under the $51,273 limit. You could get heating help paid jointly to you and your oil company, and USF credits on your electric bill if it is in your name.

Example: a retired couple in Edison

Say you and your spouse have combined income of $60,000 from Social Security and two small pensions, and you heat with gas. The limit for two people is $67,049, so you could qualify. Your heating benefit might go straight to your gas company, and the same application checks you for monthly USF credits.

What mistakes should I avoid?

  • Waiting until a cold snap. Help is first come, first served, and agencies get busy in winter.
  • Assuming you earn too much. The limits are well above the poverty line.
  • Leaving the bill in someone else's name. USF needs an electric or gas bill in a household member's name.
  • Not telling the agency about a medical need. Ask about the $300 cooling benefit if a doctor says air conditioning matters for your health.

Will this protect me from a winter shutoff?

Yes, if you are enrolled. New Jersey's Winter Termination Program protects eligible customers from gas and electric shutoffs during the cold months. Last winter it ran from November 15, 2025, through March 15, 2026. You are covered if you receive LIHEAP, USF, PAAD, Lifeline, SSI, TANF or General Assistance. Call your utility to make sure you are listed, or the Board of Public Utilities at 1-800-624-0241.

The protection pauses shutoffs. It does not erase the bill. Pay what you can each month so a large balance does not land on you in spring.

What else can help?

  • Lifeline. $225 a year toward utilities for people 65 and older, or on Social Security disability, under the PAAD income limits. See our PAAD guide.
  • NJ SHARES. Help for households that are behind on bills. Call 1-866-657-4273.
  • NJ 211. Dial 2-1-1 for other local help.

Our guide to food and utility help covers SNAP, Comfort Partners and water bills too.

faq.a: Gross income must be at or below 60% of state median income: $51,273 a year for one person, $67,049 for two and $82,825 for three.

faq.a: Yes. Households that pay a fuel supplier generally receive a check made out to both the applicant and the supplier.

title: NJ FamilyCare for seniors: the Aged, Blind, Disabled programs
dek: New Jersey's Medicaid program has its own path for people 65 and older. Here is how the Aged, Blind, Disabled programs work, the 2026 limits and how to apply.
keyFacts: For people 65+, or blind or disabled, who meet income and asset rules
2026 NJ Care Special Medicaid: $1,330 a month single, $1,804 couple
Asset limits for that program: $4,000 single, $6,000 couple
No in-person interview needed to apply
ABD application help: 1-800-356-1561
body:
NJ FamilyCare is New Jersey's name for Medicaid. Most people think of it as coverage for children and working families. It also has a separate set of programs for older adults and people with disabilities, called the Aged, Blind, Disabled (ABD) programs. If you are 65 or older with a low income and modest savings, NJ FamilyCare can work alongside Medicare and pick up many costs Medicare leaves behind.

Who can get NJ FamilyCare ABD?

  • Age or disability. You must be 65 or older, or determined blind or disabled by Social Security or the State of New Jersey.
  • Residence and status. You must live in New Jersey and be a U.S. citizen or qualified immigrant.
  • Money. Your income and countable resources must fit the rules of one of the ABD programs. A spouse's finances are considered too.

What are the ABD programs?

One application covers several programs. The county agency decides which one fits you.

  • SSI-related Medicaid. In New Jersey, people who get Supplemental Security Income (SSI) automatically receive full ABD Medicaid.
  • Medicaid Only. For people who do not get SSI but have income and resources within SSI standards.
  • New Jersey Care Special Medicaid. For people with income at or below 100% of the federal poverty level. This is the program many older adults on modest Social Security use.
  • Long Term Services and Supports. For people who need help with daily activities at home, in assisted living or in a nursing home. Most people receive it through Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS).
2026 figureSingleCouple
NJ Care Special Medicaid monthly income limit (100% of poverty level)$1,330$1,804
NJ Care Special Medicaid resource limit$4,000$6,000
Long-term care (MLTSS) monthly income limit for the applicant$2,982Ask your county

Long-term care has its own rules, including a five-year look-back at gifts and transfers. Our guide to Medicaid and MLTSS explains them in detail.

Medicare and NJ FamilyCare can work together. Having one does not rule out the other.

What does it cover?

The state's ABD brochure lists doctor and specialist visits, hospital care, prescriptions, lab tests and X-rays, rehabilitative care, mental health and substance use treatment, dental care and eyeglasses. Long-term services and supports are available to people who qualify for them.

If you have Medicare, it usually pays first. NJ FamilyCare can then help with costs Medicare does not cover. People with full Medicaid are not eligible for PAAD, but Medicaid covers prescriptions in its place.

Over the limit? Check the Medicare Savings Programs

If your income is a bit too high for NJ Care Special Medicaid, you may still get help paying your Medicare premium. The Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary and Qualifying Individual programs allow higher income, with resource limits of $9,950 for one person and $14,910 for a couple in 2026. Apply through NJSave at 1-800-792-9745. Our prescription and bill help guide has the details.

How do I apply?

Use the single NJ FamilyCare Aged, Blind, Disabled Program Application. It covers every ABD program.

  1. Choose how to apply. Apply online, or print the application and mail it. You can also get in-person help at your County Board of Social Services, also called the County Welfare Agency. The state says an in-person interview is not required.
  2. Name a helper if you want one. You can name an authorized representative, such as an adult child, to handle the application. Fill out the authorized representative form in the packet.
  3. Add supplemental forms. Married applicants may need the spousal information form.
  4. Gather proof. Expect to show identity, age, citizenship and marital status, plus records of income, resources and living expenses.
  5. Answer every letter on time. Missing a request for information can lead to a denial.

For help with the ABD application, call 1-800-356-1561. The general NJ FamilyCare hotline is 1-800-701-0710 (TTY 1-800-701-0720), open Monday and Thursday 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Example: a widow in Paterson

Say you are 79, live alone, get $1,250 a month from Social Security and have $3,000 in savings. You are under both the $1,330 income limit and the $4,000 resource limit for NJ Care Special Medicaid. Medicare would stay your main coverage, and NJ FamilyCare could help with costs Medicare leaves behind.

What mistakes slow people down?

  • Not applying because you have Medicare. Many people qualify for both.
  • Leaving out a spouse's finances. The rules look at both of you, so include everything the form asks for.
  • Missing a deadline on a letter. Open mail from the county right away. Call if you need more time.
  • Waiting for a crisis. If long-term care may be needed soon, start gathering records now.

What is estate recovery?

New Jersey can seek repayment from the estate of a member who was 55 or older when they received Medicaid services. Recovery is put off while there is a surviving spouse, a surviving child under 21, or a surviving child who is blind or permanently disabled. The state may also hold off when a family member has lived in the home continuously and still lives there. Questions go to the estate recovery unit at 609-588-2900. Our estate planning guide explains how to find an elder law attorney.

Where can I get free help?

  • Your county office on aging through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737.
  • SHIP Medicare counselors at 1-800-792-8820, who can explain how Medicare and Medicaid fit together.

If a parent is coming home from the hospital and needs care, see our hospital discharge guide.

faq.q: Can I have Medicare and NJ FamilyCare at the same time?
faq.a: Yes. Many older adults have both. Medicare usually pays first, and NJ FamilyCare helps with costs Medicare does not cover.

faq.q: What is the NJ FamilyCare income limit for seniors in 2026?
faq.a: For New Jersey Care Special Medicaid, the 2026 limit is $1,330 a month for one person and $1,804 for a couple, with resources up to $4,000 and $6,000.

faq.q: Do I have to go to an office to apply?
faq.a: No. You can apply online or by mail, and the state says an in-person interview at the County Welfare Agency is not required.

faq.q: Does New Jersey take your house after Medicaid?
faq.a: The state can seek repayment from the estate of members who were 55 or older when they got services. Recovery is postponed while a spouse or certain children survive, and may be delayed if a family member still lives in the home.

faq.q: What number do I call for help with the ABD application?
faq.a: Call 1-800-356-1561. The general NJ FamilyCare hotline is 1-800-701-0710.

title: JACC in New Jersey: home care help for seniors not on Medicaid
dek: Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving helps older adults who need a lot of care stay at home, even if they earn too much for Medicaid. Here are the 2026 rules.
keyFacts: Age 60 or older, needing nursing-home-level care
2026 income: up to $4,855 a month single, $6,582 couple
Countable assets: $40,000 single, $60,000 couple
Services up to $1,156 a month, plus care management
Apply through the ADRC: 1-877-222-3737
body:
Many families hit the same wall. A parent needs real help at home, but has too much income or savings for Medicaid and too little to pay for care for years. Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving, known as JACC, was built for that gap. It is a state program run through your county office on aging, and it helps older adults stay at home instead of moving to a nursing home.

Who qualifies for JACC in 2026?

  • Age. 60 or older.
  • Care needs. You must need nursing-facility level of care. In practice, that means needing help with at least three activities of daily living, such as bathing, toileting, dressing, moving from bed to chair, or getting around.
  • Living situation. You must live in the community in New Jersey, not in a facility.
  • Status. U.S. citizen or qualified alien.
  • Other programs. You cannot be enrolled in Medicaid programs such as NJ FamilyCare or MLTSS, or in certain other state programs such as the Statewide Respite Care Program or the Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program.
2026 financial limitSingleCouple
Monthly income (365% of the federal poverty level)$4,855$6,582
Countable assets$40,000 or less$60,000 or less
JACC is for people who need a lot of help but do not qualify for Medicaid.

Is JACC a fit for your family?

JACC is worth a call if a parent or spouse needs hands-on help most days, a family caregiver is stretched thin, and the money picture sits in the middle: too much for Medicaid, too little to pay for years of private care. If savings are already low, ask the ADRC about Medicaid at the same time. If needs are light, such as rides or a weekly check-in, other county services may fit better.

What services does JACC provide?

Everyone in JACC gets care management. A care manager assesses your needs at home and builds a care plan. Depending on that plan, it may include:

  • Home care
  • Respite care, so a family caregiver can take a break
  • Social adult day care or adult day health services
  • Home-delivered meals
  • Chore services
  • Home modifications, such as grab bars
  • A personal emergency response system
  • Specialized medical equipment and supplies
  • Transportation

Services are limited to $1,156 per participant per month, plus care management. What you actually receive depends on your assessment, your care plan and whether services and funding are available in your county.

Will I have to pay anything?

Possibly. JACC participants may be asked to pay part of the cost of services. The amount is based on income, on a sliding scale. Ask your care manager to explain your share before services begin.

Example: a father in Morristown

Say your father is 84, widowed, with $3,600 a month from Social Security and a pension and $30,000 in savings. He needs help bathing, dressing and getting around the house. His income is too high for most Medicaid programs, but he fits inside the JACC limits. A care manager might set up a few hours of home care each week, a personal emergency button and home-delivered meals.

How do I apply?

Contact your county Area Agency on Aging through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737. Staff will screen your situation and, if JACC looks like a fit, arrange an assessment at home.

  1. Call the ADRC and ask specifically about JACC.
  2. Have the numbers ready: monthly income, savings and investment balances, and insurance cards.
  3. List daily needs honestly. Write down what the person cannot do alone and how often they need help. Families often understate needs on the phone.
  4. Ask about waiting times. Services depend on funding, so ask how long the wait is in your county.
  5. Prepare for the home visit. Have medication lists and doctor names handy.

What happens at the assessment?

A care manager from your county program visits the person who needs care at home. They look at daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, toileting, moving around and eating, and they talk about memory, safety and who already helps. If the person meets the nursing-facility level of care and the financial rules, the care manager writes a care plan.

The care plan lists the services, how often they come and who provides them. It should change as needs change. If your parent's health slips, call the care manager and ask for a new look at the plan.

Questions to ask the care manager

  • Which services in the plan are available now, and which have a wait?
  • How is our cost share figured, and how will we be billed?
  • Who do we call if an aide does not show up?
  • How often will you check in, and how do we ask for changes?
  • What happens if savings drop and Medicaid becomes an option?

How does JACC compare with other options?

  • MLTSS (Medicaid). For people who meet Medicaid's financial rules. It can cover more care, but has strict income and asset limits and a five-year look-back. See our Medicaid and MLTSS guide.
  • Statewide Respite Care Program. Gives family caregivers a break. You cannot be in it and JACC at the same time. Our respite guide compares them.
  • Private home care. If you pay on your own, our guide to choosing a home care agency can help.

Where can family caregivers get support?

The state's JACC page lists several free lines for caregivers:

  • Care2Caregivers peer support: 1-800-424-2494
  • Well Spouse Association, for spouses and partners: 1-800-838-0879
  • Family Caregiver Alliance: 1-800-445-8106

If memory loss is part of the picture, see our dementia support guide.

faq.q: What is JACC in New Jersey?
faq.a: Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving is a state program that provides home and community services to people 60 and older who need nursing-home-level care but are not on Medicaid.

faq.q: What are the JACC income limits for 2026?
faq.a: Monthly income can be up to $4,855 for a single person or $6,582 for a couple. Countable assets must be $40,000 or less for one person or $60,000 for a couple.

faq.q: How much does JACC pay for services?
faq.a: Services are limited to $1,156 per participant per month, plus care management. Participants may pay a share based on income, on a sliding scale.

faq.q: Can I be on JACC and Medicaid at the same time?
faq.a: No. JACC serves people who are not enrolled in Medicaid programs such as NJ FamilyCare or MLTSS.

faq.q: How do I apply for JACC?
faq.a: Call your county Area Agency on Aging through the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737. A care manager will assess needs at home.

NJ Division of Aging Services: County offices on aging

title: Meals on Wheels in NJ: home-delivered meals by county
dek: If getting groceries or cooking has become hard, your county can deliver meals to adults 60 and older. Here is who qualifies, what it costs and who to call in each of New Jersey's 21 counties.
keyFacts: For adults 60+ who are homebound by illness, disability or isolation
At least one meal a day, five days a week
A needs assessment is required
Federally funded meals ask for a suggested contribution
Statewide line: 1-877-222-3737
body:
Home-delivered meals, often called Meals on Wheels, bring a hot meal to the door of older adults who have a hard time shopping or cooking. In New Jersey, the main program runs through each county's Area Agency on Aging, also called the county office on aging. It is funded largely with federal dollars, and you are asked for a contribution only if you can afford one.

The driver's visit matters too. For someone who lives alone, it can be a daily friendly face and a quick check that all is well.

Who qualifies for home-delivered meals?

  • Age. 60 or older.
  • Homebound. You are homebound because of illness, disability or isolation.
  • Assessment. A formal needs assessment must be done before meals start. Someone from the county program will ask about your health, how you get food now and who helps you.
  • Spouses. Meals may also be provided for a spouse if it supports the homebound person.

Each county sets its own details within the program rules, such as delivery days and waiting lists. That is why the first call should go to your county office.

What do I get, and what does it cost?

Programs deliver at least one hot meal a day, five days a week. Some offer weekend and holiday meals for people who qualify. Federally funded programs ask for a suggested contribution. Ask your county what it suggests and how contributions work if money is tight.

Start with one phone call to your county office on aging.

Who do I call in my county?

Call your county office on aging and ask for the home-delivered meals or nutrition program. These are the county offices listed by the New Jersey Division of Aging Services. If you are calling for a parent, call the county where your parent lives.

How does signing up work?

  1. Call your county office. Say you are asking about home-delivered meals. Give the name, address and phone of the person who needs them.
  2. Do the screening. Expect questions about health, mobility, diet and whether anyone helps with meals.
  3. Mention special diets. Ask what options are available, such as meals for diabetes or low salt.
  4. Ask about timing. Some counties have waiting lists. Ask how long it will be and what to do meanwhile.
  5. Plan for the door. Make sure someone can answer, or tell the program about any access issues.
Example: a mother in Clifton

Say your mother is 86, lives alone in Passaic County and stopped cooking after a fall. You call the Passaic County Department of Senior Services at 973-569-4060. Staff schedule an assessment, and if she qualifies, a meal arrives on weekdays. You ask whether weekend meals are possible and fill in Saturday and Sunday yourself until then.

Are there other ways to get meals?

Group meals at senior centers

If you can get out, congregate meals are open to anyone 60 or older and their spouse of any age. Senior centers, churches and community sites serve at least one hot meal a day, five or more days a week. You contribute what you can. Many sites ask you to reserve 24 hours ahead. It is also a good way to see people.

Meals through Medicaid or JACC

Home-delivered meals can be part of a care plan under Medicaid's Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) and under JACC, the state program for people who need a lot of care but are not on Medicaid. See our MLTSS guide and our JACC guide.

Local nonprofit meal programs

Some towns have their own nonprofit meal delivery groups. Some serve people of any age and may charge a set fee. Your county office or NJ 211 (dial 2-1-1) can tell you what operates near you.

Food benefits

SNAP can help pay for groceries, and the rules are friendlier for people 60 and older. Our guide to food and utility help explains how to apply.

Tips for families

  • Call before a crisis. If a parent is losing weight or the fridge is emptier each visit, call now.
  • Ask the hospital. If a parent is being discharged, ask the discharge planner to start a meals referral. Our hospital discharge guide covers what else to ask for.
  • Keep the county informed. Tell the program about hospital stays or trips so meals are paused.
  • Look at the bigger picture. Meals are often the first sign that more help is needed. Our guide to aging in place covers other supports.

faq.q: Who is eligible for Meals on Wheels in New Jersey?
faq.a: Adults 60 and older who are homebound because of illness, disability or isolation. A needs assessment is required, and a spouse may also receive meals if it supports the homebound person.

faq.q: How much do home-delivered meals cost in NJ?
faq.a: Federally funded programs ask for a suggested contribution. Ask your county office on aging what it suggests and how contributions work.

faq.q: How many meals are delivered?
faq.a: Programs deliver at least one hot meal a day, five days a week. Some offer weekend and holiday meals for eligible participants.

faq.q: How do I sign up a parent for Meals on Wheels?
faq.a: Call the county office on aging where your parent lives, or the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737, and ask for the home-delivered meals program.

faq.q: Are there meals for seniors who can still get out?
faq.a: Yes. Congregate meals at senior centers and community sites are open to anyone 60 or older and their spouse. You contribute what you can, and many sites ask you to reserve a day ahead.
